u1.title: DNA Profiling and Forensic Analysis using PCR
u1.description: A diagram explaining DNA fingerprinting for forensic identification. It illustrates the analysis of three specific loci across three pairs of homologous chromosomes for Individuals A, B, C, and a forensic sample F. Following PCR amplification and gel electrophoresis, the DNA fragments are separated by size (number of repeats). The resulting banding pattern on the electrophoresis gel shows that forensic sample F is a perfect match for Individual B, demonstrating how molecular tools are used to identify suspects.

u1.title: The Role of Microorganisms in Wastewater Treatment
u1.description: A flowchart detailing the stages of biological sewage treatment. Primary treatment involves physical removal via bar screens and grit tanks. Secondary treatment utilizes microbial oxidation through trickling filters or activated sludge to break down organic matter. The process yields treated water, which is disinfected via chlorination or UV treatment before discharge, and sludge, which undergoes anaerobic digestion to produce CO2 and methane (CH4) before final dewatering and disposal.

u1.title: Genetic Engineering of Plants via Ti Plasmid Vectors
u1.description: A five-step process for creating transgenic, herbicide-resistant plants. (1) A leaf is cut; (2) it is exposed to a bacterial suspension carrying a Ti plasmid with glyphosate and antibiotic resistance genes; (3) cells are grown on an antibiotic medium where only those that successfully incorporated the new DNA survive to form a callus; (4) the callus is stimulated to sprout shoots and roots; and (5) the plant is transferred to soil, resulting in a mature, glyphosate-resistant adult plant.

u1.title: Plant Tissue Culture and Micropropagation
u1.description: A four-step diagram illustrating the process of tissue culture (micropropagation). First, a tissue sample is scraped from a parent plant leaf. Second, the samples are placed in a Petri dish containing an agar growth medium with essential nutrients and auxins (plant hormones). Third, the samples develop into tiny plantlets under controlled conditions. Finally, the plantlets are transplanted into a compost box for further growth, demonstrating how genetically identical clones of a parent plant are produced in a laboratory setting.

u1.title: Methane Generator and Anaerobic Digestion
u1.description: A cross-section diagram of a methane generator used for the anaerobic digestion of organic waste. Raw materials including sewage, animal manure, farm waste, and garden waste enter the chamber. Inside, under anaerobic (oxygen-free) conditions, microorganisms decompose the matter to produce methane gas, which is captured at the top for use in cooking, heating, or refrigeration. The remaining liquid byproduct, called slurry, is collected from an outlet to be used as a nutrient-rich fertilizer.

u1.title: Industrial Enzyme Production from Micro-organisms
u1.description: A process flow diagram showing the industrial production of enzymes. In the fermenter tank, feedstock and microorganisms are stirred by paddles while air is supplied, and waste gases are vented. The mixture moves to a filtration stage where microorganisms are separated from the filtrate. The diagram distinguishes between two extraction methods: extracellular enzymes are harvested from the liquid filtrate, while intracellular enzymes are extracted directly from the separated microorganisms.

u1.title: Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer: The Cloning of Dolly the Sheep
u1.description: A detailed diagram illustrating the process of somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT). First, udder cells are taken from a donor sheep while unfertilized egg cells are taken from a second sheep. The nucleus is removed from the egg cell using a micropipette to create an enucleated egg. This egg is then fused with the donor udder cell using a pulse of electricity. The fused cell develops into an embryo and is implanted into a surrogate mother. The process results in the birth of Dolly, a lamb genetically identical to the original udder cell donor, demonstrating the first successful cloning of a mammal from an adult somatic cell.

u2.title: Universal Phylogenetic Tree of Life
u2.description: A universal phylogenetic tree constructed from small subunit rRNA gene sequence analysis, showing the three domains of life: Bacteria (blue), Archaea (red), and Eukaryota (brown), all originating from the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA).

u2.title: Major Features of a Prokaryotic Cell (Bacteria)
u2.description: A labeled diagram of a bacterial prokaryotic cell highlighting key structures including the peptidoglycan cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleoid containing the genophore, plasmid, ribosomes, slime capsule (glycocalyx), pili, and flagella.

u2.title: Major Features of a Eukaryotic Cell
u2.description: A detailed labeled diagram of a eukaryotic cell showing organelles including the nucleus, nucleolus, endoplasmic reticulum (smooth and rough), Golgi body, mitochondria, ribosomes, lysosomes, peroxisomes, cytoskeleton, cytosol, and plasma membrane.

u2.title: Basic Bacterial Shapes and Clustering
u2.description: An illustrated chart showing the three basic bacterial morphologies: Cocci (spherical forms including coccus, diplococci, tetrad, sarcina, streptococci, staphylococci), Bacilli (rod forms including coccobacillus, bacillus, diplobacilli, streptobacilli, palisades), and Others (spirilla, corynebacterium, vibrios, spirochete).

u2.title: Gram Positive and Gram Negative Bacterial Cell Wall
u2.description: A comparative 3D diagram illustrating the structural differences between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial cell walls. Gram-positive walls feature thick peptidoglycan with teichoic and lipoteichoic acids, while Gram-negative walls have a thinner peptidoglycan layer, periplasmic space, and an outer membrane with lipopolysaccharides, porins, and phospholipids.

u2.title: Gram Staining Process
u2.description: A step-by-step visual guide to the Gram staining procedure showing the sequential application of fixation, crystal violet, iodine treatment, decolorization, and safranin counter stain. Gram-positive bacteria retain the purple crystal violet stain, while Gram-negative bacteria appear pink/red after safranin.

u2.title: The Process of Binary Fission
u2.description: A four-step diagram illustrating bacterial binary fission: (1) cell elongation and DNA replication, (2) invagination of cell wall and membrane with fission ring apparatus formation, (3) cross-wall formation creating two distinct cells, and (4) complete cell separation.

u2.title: Bacterial Conjugation
u2.description: A four-step diagram of bacterial conjugation showing: (1) F+ donor cell producing a sex pilus toward an F- recipient cell, (2) sex pilus developing into a conjugation bridge, (3) DNA replication and transfer of a single-stranded F plasmid from F+ to F- cell, and (4) both cells ending up with double-stranded F plasmid, converting the F- cell to F+.

u2.title: Classes of Microbes Based on Physical Factors
u2.description: A comprehensive flowchart categorizing microbes according to four physical growth factors: temperature (psychrophiles, psychrotrophs, mesophiles, thermophiles, hyperthermophiles), oxygen (obligate aerobes, microaerophiles, facultative, aerotolerant, obligate anaerobes), pH (acidophiles), and osmotic conditions (halotolerant, nonhalophiles, halophiles, extreme halophiles).

u2.title: Fungal Mycelium Structure
u2.description: A diagram of fungal mycelium showing the structural components: sporangia (spore-bearing structures) atop sporangiophores, connected by stolons running along the surface, with rhizoids extending below the surface for anchorage and nutrient absorption.

u2.title: Sexual Reproduction Cycle of a Typical Basidiomycete
u2.description: A circular life cycle diagram of a basidiomycete mushroom showing: basidiospore germination into haploid mycelium, fusion of opposite mating strains into heterokaryotic mycelium, emergence as a mushroom (basidiocarp), formation of basidia on gill surfaces, nuclear fusion to form a zygote, meiosis to produce haploid basidiospores, and their subsequent release.

u2.title: Common Protozoa
u2.description: An illustrated overview of common protozoa grouped by locomotion type. Class Rhizopodea (pseudopodia): Amoeba, Entamoeba. Class Mastigophora (flagella): Euglena, Noctiluca, Trypanosoma, Giardia. Class Ciliata (cilia): Paramecium, Opalina, Monocystis.

u2.title: Asexual Reproduction in Protozoa
u2.description: A diagram illustrating four modes of asexual reproduction in protozoa: longitudinal binary fission (as in flagellates), binary fission in amoeba, multiple fission/schizogony (as in Plasmodium, the malaria parasite, inside blood cells), and transverse binary fission (involving micronucleus and macronucleus, as in ciliates).

u2.title: Conjugation in Paramecium
u2.description: A detailed cycle diagram of sexual reproduction (conjugation) in Paramecium showing nine steps: alignment and partial fusion of compatible mates, meiosis of micronuclei producing four haploid micronuclei, disintegration of three micronuclei, mitotic division of the remaining one, reciprocal micronucleus exchange, separation, micronuclear fusion, mitosis producing eight micronuclei, four becoming macronuclei, and two rounds of binary fission yielding four daughter cells.

u2.title: Size Variations Among Cells and Viruses
u2.description: A size comparison illustration showing the relative scale of a eukaryotic cell (10,000 nm), cell nucleus (2,800 nm), bacterium E. coli (2,000 nm), and various viruses including smallpox (250 nm), tobacco mosaic (240 nm), rabies (150 nm), influenza (100 nm), bacteriophage (95 nm), common cold (70 nm), polio (28 nm), and parvovirus (20 nm).

u2.title: Bacteriophage Structure
u2.description: A labeled structural diagram of a bacteriophage showing its key components: a hexagonal head containing the DNA core, a tail with a base plate, prongs, and tail fibers used for host cell attachment.

u2.title: Variations in Shapes and Sizes of Viruses
u2.description: A comparative illustration showing diverse virus morphologies (poxvirus, togavirus, herpesvirus, T4 bacteriophage, reovirus, adenovirus, picornavirus, tobacco mosaic virus, paramyxovirus) displayed within the context of an E. coli bacterial cell, a human liver cell, and a eukaryotic ribosome to provide scale.

u2.title: The Lytic Cycle of Phage T4
u2.description: A circular diagram of the lytic replication cycle of bacteriophage T4 illustrating five stages: (1) attachment to host cell, (2) penetration and injection of phage DNA with degradation of host DNA, (3) replication of phage DNA, (4) assembly of new phage particles with synthesis of structural proteins, and (5) release of new phage particles through host cell lysis.

u2.title: Lysogenic Bacteriophage Cycle
u2.description: A combined diagram of both the lytic and lysogenic cycles of a temperate bacteriophage. The lysogenic cycle shows phage DNA integrating as a prophage into the bacterial chromosome, replicating with the host through binary fission, and potentially undergoing induction to enter the lytic cycle, which proceeds through adsorption, penetration, biosynthesis, maturation, and release.

u2.title: Normal Microbiota of the Human Body
u2.description: An anatomical diagram of the female human body annotating the normal microbial flora at key sites: oral cavity (Streptococcus, Treponema, Neisseria, Haemophilus, Lactobacillus, Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium), upper respiratory tract (Streptococcus, Neisseria, Haemophilus, Staphylococcus; fungal: Candida), skin (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Corynebacterium, Propionibacterium, Micrococcus; fungal: Candida), urinary tract (Lactobacillus, Corynebacterium, Streptococcus, Bacteroides in females; Corynebacterium, Streptococcus in males), intestines (Bacteroides, Lactobacillus, Streptococcus in small intestine; dense populations in large intestine), and female reproductive tract (Lactobacillus, Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, Streptococcus, Enterococcus; fungal: Candida).

u2.title: Koch's Postulates for Identifying Pathogens
u2.description: A diagram illustrating the four fundamental criteria used to establish a causative relationship between a microbe and a disease. Postulate 1: The same microorganisms are present in every case of the disease (shown in a diseased sheep). Postulate 2: The microorganisms are isolated from the dead animal and grown in a pure culture. Postulate 3: Microorganisms from the pure culture are inoculated into a healthy, susceptible animal (mouse), reproducing the disease. Postulate 4: The identical microorganisms are re-isolated and recultivated from the experimental animal, confirming the pathogen.

u2.title: Recombinant DNA Technology for Human Insulin Production
u2.description: A process flow diagram showing how human insulin is produced using transgenic bacteria. A specific human insulin gene is isolated and inserted into a bacterial plasmid to create a recombinant plasmid. This plasmid is introduced into a bacterium, which is then grown in large cultures. As the transgenic bacteria multiply, they produce human insulin protein, which is finally extracted and purified for medical use in treating diabetes.

u2.title: The Microbial Carbon Cycle: Aerobic and Anaerobic Pathways
u2.description: A complex diagram illustrating how carbon moves through different chemical forms and environments. In aerobic conditions (blue), CO2 is fixed into organic compounds, which are then returned to CO2 via aerobic respiration. In anaerobic conditions (pink), carbon fixation occurs alongside anaerobic respiration and fermentation. The diagram also highlights the methane cycle: methanogenesis (the reduction of CO2 to CH4 in anaerobic environments) and methane oxidation (the oxidation of CH4 back to CO2 as an energy source in aerobic environments).

u2.title: The Microbial Nitrogen Cycle
u2.description: A complex diagram illustrating the biochemical transformations of nitrogen. Key processes include nitrogen fixation (N2 to NH3), nitrification (oxidation of NH3 to NO2- and NO3-), and denitrification (reduction of NO3- back to N2). It also shows assimilation into protein NH2 groups, ammonification of organic matter, and specialized pathways like Anammox (anaerobic ammonium oxidation) and DRNA (dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium), distinguishing between oxic and anoxic conditions.

u2.title: The Microbial Sulfur Cycle
u2.description: A diagram showing the cycling of sulfur compounds in oxic and anoxic environments. It details the oxidation of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and elemental sulfur (S0) to sulfate (SO4 2-) via chemolithotrophic oxidation. The reverse process, sulfate reduction, is shown alongside sulfate assimilation into protein SH groups. The cycle also includes the interconversion of organic sulfur compounds like DMS (dimethyl sulfide) and DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide).

u2.title: The Phosphorus Cycle in Soil and Ecosystems
u2.description: An environmental diagram mapping phosphorus movement through the soil-plant system. Inputs include mineral fertilizers, atmospheric deposition, and animal manures. The diagram tracks 'Soluble P' (H2PO4- and HPO4 2-) through processes like plant uptake, immobilization into organic forms (microbial/humus), and mineralization. It also illustrates chemical interactions such as adsorption/desorption on mineral surfaces and losses via crop harvest, runoff, and erosion.

u3.title: Metabolic Pathways: Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration
u3.description: A diagram showing the interconnection between photosynthesis (occurring in the chloroplast) and aerobic cellular respiration (occurring in the mitochondrion). Photosynthesis uses sunlight, H2O, and CO2 to produce O2 and glucose, while cellular respiration consumes glucose and O2 to produce H2O, CO2, and ATP from ADP.

u3.title: External Structure of a Leaf
u3.description: A labeled diagram of the external morphology of a leaf showing the tip, midrib, margin, vein, lamina (blade), and petiole (stalk).

u3.title: Internal Structure of a Leaf
u3.description: A multi-panel diagram of leaf internal anatomy including: (a) a 3D cutaway showing dermal, ground, and vascular tissue layers with cuticle, sclerenchyma fibres, stoma, bundle sheath cells, xylem, phloem, vein, and guard cells; (b) a surface view LM of Tradescantia showing guard cells, stomatal pore, and epidermal cells; and (c) a cross-section LM of a Syringa leaf showing upper/lower epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, veins, air spaces, and guard cells.

u3.title: Chloroplast Structure and Location in a Plant Cell
u3.description: A multi-scale diagram tracing from a whole plant to a leaf cross section showing chloroplasts in the mesophyll cell layer, then to a single mesophyll cell, and finally a detailed chloroplast structure labeled with stroma, thylakoid, granum, thylakoid space, inner membrane, outer membrane, and intermembrane space. Stomata exchanging CO2 and O2 are also shown.

u3.title: Absorption Spectrum of Photosynthetic Pigments
u3.description: A graph plotting the amount of light absorbed (y-axis) against wavelength of light in nm (x-axis, 400–700 nm) for three pigments: Chlorophyll a (dark green, with peaks near 430 nm and 680 nm), Chlorophyll b (lighter green, with peaks near 460 nm and 640 nm), and Carotenoids (yellow-orange, with peak absorption between 400–500 nm).

u3.title: Light-Dependent Reaction: Non-Cyclic Photophosphorylation
u3.description: A diagram of the non-cyclic (Z-scheme) light-dependent reaction of photosynthesis showing electron flow from water splitting at Photosystem II (P680), through electron carriers QA, QB, the cytochrome complex, and plastocyanin (Pc) to Photosystem I (P700), then via ferredoxin (Fd) and NADP+ reductase to produce NADPH. Water is split releasing O2 and H+ ions.

u3.title: Light-Dependent Reaction: Cyclic Photophosphorylation
u3.description: A diagram illustrating cyclic photophosphorylation in photosynthesis, where a photon excites the reaction center (P870), boosting electrons to high energy. Electrons cycle through electron acceptors and the b-c1 complex, releasing energy to synthesize ATP, before returning to the reaction center. No NADPH or O2 is produced.

u3.title: Calvin Cycle (C3 Cycle)
u3.description: A circular diagram of the Calvin-Benson cycle showing three phases: (1) CO2 uptake phase — 6 CO2 molecules are fixed by RuBP to form 12 molecules of phosphoglycerate (PGA); (2) Carbon reduction phase — PGA is phosphorylated by ATP and reduced by NADPH to form glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P); (3) RuBP regeneration phase — 10 G3P molecules regenerate 6 RuBP molecules using ATP. 2 G3P are used for glucose and carbohydrate synthesis.

u3.title: The C4 Photosynthetic Pathway
u3.description: A detailed biochemical diagram of C4 photosynthesis occurring across mesophyll and bundle sheath cells. In the mesophyll cell, atmospheric CO2 is converted to HCO3- by carbonic anhydrase, then fixed by PEP carboxylase to form oxaloacetate, which is reduced to malate. Malate is transported to the bundle sheath cell where malic enzyme releases CO2 for the Calvin cycle and regenerates pyruvate, which returns to the mesophyll cell and is converted back to PEP by pyruvate-phosphate dikinase using ATP.

u3.title: CAM Cycle
u3.description: A two-panel diagram comparing CAM (Crassulacean Acid Metabolism) photosynthesis at night (stomata open) and during the day (stomata closed). At night, open stomata allow CO2 entry; PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 to form oxaloacetate then malate, which is stored as malic acid in the vacuole. During the day, closed stomata prevent water loss; stored malic acid is decarboxylated by NADP+ malic enzyme, releasing CO2 for the Calvin cycle in the chloroplast and generating pyruvate and starch.

u3.title: The Photorespiratory Cycle
u3.description: A detailed metabolic diagram of the photorespiratory (C2) cycle spanning three organelles. In the chloroplast, RuBP oxygenation produces 2-phosphoglycolate and 3-phosphoglycerate via the Calvin-Benson cycle. In the peroxisome, glycolate is oxidized to glyoxylate and then glycine. In the mitochondria, two glycine molecules are converted to serine with release of CO2 and NH3. Serine returns to the peroxisome and then to the chloroplast as glycerate, re-entering the Calvin cycle.

u3.title: Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) Structure
u3.description: A structural diagram of an ATP molecule showing its three components: one adenine nitrogenous base (purine ring), one ribose sugar, and three phosphate groups linked in sequence. The high-energy bonds between the phosphate groups are the source of chemical energy for cellular processes.

u3.title: ATP Cycle
u3.description: A cyclic diagram illustrating the ATP-ADP energy cycle. ATP synthesis (endergonic) uses energy from exergonic chemical reactions to combine ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) into ATP. ATP hydrolysis (exergonic) releases energy to drive endergonic cellular processes, regenerating ADP and Pi.

u3.title: Stages of Cellular Respiration
u3.description: An overview diagram of the four stages of aerobic cellular respiration located within a mitochondrion: (1) Glycolysis in the cytosol producing pyruvate and 2 ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation; (2) Formation of Acetyl Coenzyme A, transferring electrons via NADH; (3) Citric acid cycle producing 2 ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation with electrons carried by NADH and FADH2; (4) Electron transport chain and chemiosmosis producing 32 ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.

u3.title: Glycolysis Pathway
u3.description: A detailed step-by-step diagram of the 10-step glycolysis pathway converting one glucose molecule to two pyruvate molecules. Steps include: phosphorylation of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase), isomerization to fructose-6-phosphate (phosphoglucoisomerase), second phosphorylation to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (phosphofructokinase), cleavage into DHAP and G3P (aldolase/isomerase), oxidation to 1,3-BPG producing NADH, substrate-level phosphorylation yielding ATP and 3-PG, and further reactions via enolase and pyruvate kinase to produce pyruvate. Structural formulas are shown on the right.

u3.title: Pyruvate Oxidation (Link Reaction)
u3.description: A diagram of the pyruvate oxidation link reaction showing pyruvate being transported from the cytosol into the mitochondrion via a transport protein. Inside the mitochondrion, three simultaneous steps occur: (1) decarboxylation releasing CO2, (2) oxidation of NAD+ to NADH, and (3) attachment of coenzyme A to form Acetyl CoA, which enters the citric acid cycle.

u3.title: Citric Acid Cycle (Krebs Cycle)
u3.description: A circular diagram of the citric acid cycle showing Acetyl CoA combining with oxaloacetate to form citrate (6C), which is progressively oxidized through a 5-carbon compound and a 4-carbon compound back to oxaloacetate. The cycle produces 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP (converted to ATP), and releases 2 CO2 per turn.

u3.title: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
u3.description: A diagram of the inner mitochondrial membrane showing the electron transport chain complexes (I–IV) and ATP synthase. NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the chain, driving proton (H+) pumping from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space. Electrons ultimately reduce O2 to H2O at Complex IV. The proton gradient drives H+ back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis) to synthesize ATP from ADP and Pi.

u3.title: Energy Yield Per Glucose Molecule
u3.description: A summary flow diagram of the total ATP yield from complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule: glycolysis yields 2 ATP (substrate-level) + 2 NADH (→4 ATP); pyruvate oxidation yields 2 NADH (→6 ATP); Krebs cycle yields 2 ATP + 6 NADH (→18 ATP) + 2 FADH2 (→4 ATP). Total net ATP yield = 36 ATP.

u3.title: Catabolism of Various Food Molecules
u3.description: A flowchart showing how the three major macromolecule classes are catabolized and fed into cellular respiration. Proteins are broken down to amino acids, carbohydrates to sugars (entering glycolysis as glucose or glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate), and fats to glycerol and fatty acids (entering as acetyl CoA). All pathways converge at Acetyl CoA, then proceed through the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation to generate ATP.

u3.title: Alcohol Fermentation Pathway in Yeast
u3.description: A biochemical diagram illustrating alcohol fermentation. Through glycolysis, glucose is converted into two pyruvate molecules, yielding a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. In the fermentation stage, pyruvate undergoes decarboxylation to form two acetaldehyde molecules, releasing 2 CO2 as a byproduct (relevant to baking). Acetaldehyde then accepts electrons from NADH to produce two ethanol molecules (relevant to brewing), which regenerates NAD+ for continued glycolysis.

u3.title: Lactic Acid Fermentation Pathway in Humans
u3.description: A biochemical diagram showing the process of lactic acid fermentation. Glucose is broken down into two pyruvate molecules, producing 2 ATP and 2 NADH. Unlike alcohol fermentation, there is no intermediate step; pyruvate directly accepts electrons from NADH to form lactic acid (lactate). This pathway is used by human muscle cells during intense exercise to regenerate NAD+, allowing ATP production via glycolysis to continue when oxygen levels are low.

u4.title: Pasteur's Experiment Disproving Spontaneous Generation
u4.description: A five-step diagram of Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment: (1) broth is boiled to sterilize it, (2) sterilized broth cools while microbes from outside are trapped in the bent neck, (3) broth remains sterile, (4) when the flask is tilted so broth contacts microbes in the neck, and (5) microbes replicate in the broth, demonstrating that life comes from pre-existing life, not spontaneous generation.

u4.title: Stanley Miller's Spark-Discharge Experiment
u4.description: A labeled diagram of the Miller-Urey apparatus used to simulate early Earth conditions. Gases (CH4, NH3, H2O, H2) are circulated through a spark chamber with electrodes providing electrical discharge. Steam from boiling water drives circulation, and products condense through a water-cooled condenser into a trap collecting water containing organic compounds. The experiment demonstrated that organic molecules can form abiotically.

u4.title: Evolution of Life and Oxygen on Earth
u4.description: A graph showing atmospheric oxygen levels (%) over 4.6 billion years of Earth's history. Key events are annotated on a timeline: formation of Earth (4.6 Bya), formation of oceans and continents (3.8 Bya), first living cells (3.5 Bya), first photosynthetic cells releasing O2 (3.0 Bya), start of rapid O2 accumulation (2.4 Bya), aerobic respiration becomes widespread (1.8 Bya), first multicellular plants and animals (0.6 Bya), and first vertebrates, up to present day at ~21% O2.

u4.title: Homologous Forelimbs of Mammals
u4.description: A comparative anatomy diagram showing the homologous bone structures in the forelimbs of four mammals: human (arm/hand), cat (foreleg), whale (flipper), and bat (wing). All share the same basic skeletal elements — humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges — color-coded identically, demonstrating common ancestry despite different functions and shapes.

u4.title: Similarities in Embryonic Development
u4.description: A comparative embryology diagram showing the early embryos of four vertebrates — fish, reptile, bird, and human — at similar developmental stages. All four embryos show gill slits and a tail, illustrating that distantly related vertebrates share common developmental pathways and evolutionary ancestry.

u4.title: Half-Life of a Radioactive Element
u4.description: A decay curve graph plotting the percentage of radioactive atoms remaining (y-axis, 0–100%) against the number of half-lives elapsed (x-axis, 0–6). Crystal diagrams illustrate the progressive decay: 0% decayed (newly formed), 25% decayed, 50% decayed (at 1 half-life, marked with red lines), 75% decayed, and 96.88% decayed at 5 half-lives.

u4.title: Carbon-14 Dating Curve
u4.description: A graph converting the percentage of original carbon-14 remaining (y-axis) to the age of a fossil in years (x-axis, 0–28,650 years). The exponential decay curve shows that at 5,730 years one half-life has elapsed (50% C-14 remains), at 11,460 years 25% remains, at 17,910 years 12.5% remains, and so on, enabling age determination of organic fossils.

u4.title: Types of Natural Selection
u4.description: A four-panel diagram using beetle wing color distributions to illustrate modes of natural selection: (a) No selection — normal distribution of phenotypes under polygenic control; (b) Stabilizing selection — extreme phenotypes are eliminated, reducing variation around the mean; (c) Directional selection — the distribution shifts toward one extreme, changing the average phenotype; (d) Disruptive selection — intermediate phenotypes are eliminated, producing two or more distinct peaks.

u4.title: Drug Resistance in Bacteria via Genetic Mutation
u4.description: A four-step diagram showing the evolution of antibiotic resistance: non-resistant bacteria exist in a population; bacteria multiply by the billions and a few undergo DNA mutations; in the presence of drugs, only drug-resistant mutants survive; drug-resistant bacteria then multiply and thrive, demonstrating natural selection acting on random mutations.

u4.title: Types of Evolution
u4.description: A diagram illustrating three patterns of evolutionary change over time: (A) Divergent evolution — one parent species splits into two or more distinct lineages; (B) Convergent evolution — two separate parent species independently evolve similar traits; (C) Parallel evolution — two related parent species evolve similarly but independently in the same direction.

u4.title: Allopatric vs. Sympatric Speciation
u4.description: A comparative diagram contrasting two modes of speciation: (i) Allopatric speciation, where geographic isolation (e.g., a mountain barrier) physically separates a population, leading to reproductive isolation and new species; and (ii) Sympatric speciation, where reproductive isolation arises within the same geographic area without physical barriers.

u4.title: Evolutionary Tree of Modern Primates
u4.description: A phylogenetic tree showing the divergence times (in millions of years ago) among modern primates. Two main suborders are shown: Strepsirrhini (Lemur) and Haplorhini (Tarsius, and the simians). Simians are divided into Platyrrhini/New World monkeys (Callithrix, Saimiri, Pithecia, Lagothrix) and Catarrhini/Old World monkeys and apes (Macaca, Colobus, Hylobates, Pongo, Gorilla, Pan, Homo), with divergence times spanning the Eocene, Oligocene, and Miocene to Holocene epochs.

u4.title: Evolutionary Tree of Humans and Great Apes
u4.description: A timed phylogenetic tree showing the evolutionary divergence of five hominids: Orangutan (48 chromosomes), Gorilla (48), Chimpanzee (48), Bonobo (48), and Human (46 chromosomes). Key branching points: common ancestor of all five at ~13 Mya, gorilla split at ~8 Mya, chimpanzee-human split at ~6 Mya, and chimpanzee-bonobo split at ~3 Mya.

u4.title: Timeline for Major Hominin and Hominid Species
u4.description: A hierarchical phylogenetic timeline spanning 25 million years ago to present, organizing primate groups from broad to narrow: Catarrhines (Cercopithecoids and Hominoids), Hominoids (apes and humans), Hominids (great apes and humans), and Hominins (the human lineage). Fossil genera shown include Ekembo, Nacholapithecus, Nakalipithecus, Sivapithecus, Dryopith apes, and Ardipithecus, with extant groups including Old World monkeys, Hylobatids, Pongo, Gorilla, Pan, and Homo.

u4.title: Fossil Timeline of the Human Family
u4.description: A comprehensive timeline from 7 million years ago to today showing the fossil record of human ancestors across geological epochs (Miocene, Pliocene, Pleistocene, Holocene). Genera represented include Sahelanthropus (S. tchadensis/Toumaï), Orrorin (O. tugenensis/Millennium Man), Ardipithecus (Ar. kadabba, Ar. ramidus/Ardi), Australopithecus (Au. anamensis, Au. afarensis/Lucy, Au. africanus/Taung Child, Au. bahrelghazali/Abel, Au. garhi, Au. aethiopicus, Au. robustus, Au. boisei, Au. rudolfensis), Kenyanthropus platyops, and Homo (H. habilis, H. erectus, H. heidelbergensis, H. neanderthalensis, H. floresiensis, H. sapiens).

u4.title: Brain Size in Different Hominids
u4.description: A graph plotting cranial capacity (cm³, y-axis) against time in millions of years before present (x-axis), showing brain size increase across hominid evolution. Skull illustrations with yellow brain regions are shown for: Antropoide (~10 Mya), Australopithecus africanus (~3–4 Mya, ~500 cm³), Homo habilis (~2 Mya), Homo erectus (~1.5 Mya, ~1000 cm³), Homo sapiens neanderthalensis, and Homo sapiens sapiens (~1500 cm³). The hominid phase shows a dramatic exponential increase in brain size.

u4.title: Types of Point Mutation
u4.description: A diagram illustrating three types of DNA point mutations using a color-coded nucleotide sequence: (1) Base substitution — one nucleotide (T) is replaced by another (C), altering a single codon; (2) Base addition — an extra nucleotide (C) is inserted, causing a frameshift in all downstream codons; (3) Base deletion — a nucleotide (T) is removed, also causing a frameshift in downstream codons.

u4.title: Types of Chromosomal Mutations
u4.description: A four-panel diagram illustrating chromosomal-level mutations using labeled gene segments (A–F): (1) Duplication — a segment (B) is copied and repeated; (2) Deletion — a segment (C) is lost from the chromosome; (3) Inversion — a segment (B–E) is reversed in orientation; (4) Translocation — segments (b, c, d, e, f, g) from one chromosome are transferred to a non-homologous chromosome.

u4.title: Genetic Drift in a Rabbit Population
u4.description: A three-generation diagram demonstrating genetic drift in a rabbit population. In the first generation, allele frequencies are p(B)=0.5 and q(b)=0.5 among brown (BB, Bb) and white (bb) rabbits. After only 5 rabbits reproduce, the second generation shifts to p=0.7 and q=0.3. After only 2 rabbits reproduce, the third generation reaches fixation at p=1 and q=0, with all rabbits being BB — illustrating how random chance can eliminate alleles in small populations.

u4.title: Bottleneck Effect
u4.description: A diagram illustrating the bottleneck effect using colored balls (yellow and blue) representing alleles in a population. A large, genetically diverse parent population passes through a bottleneck event (drastic population reduction), leaving only a few surviving individuals. The next generation, rebuilt from survivors, shows a drastically altered and reduced allele frequency — predominantly blue — demonstrating loss of genetic diversity through random sampling.

u4.title: The Founder Effect and Genetic Diversity
u4.description: A diagram illustrating the founder effect, a form of genetic drift. A large, genetically diverse source population (represented by many colored balls) serves as the origin for three smaller 'founder' populations. When small groups colonize a new area, they carry only a random subset of the original population's alleles. As a result, the new populations have significantly different and reduced genetic diversity compared to the parent group, with some alleles becoming fixed and others being eliminated entirely by chance.

u4.title: Gene Flow via Immigration
u4.description: A diagram illustrating gene flow between two distinct beetle populations. One population is composed of green beetles, while the other is composed of brown beetles. A brown beetle is shown migrating (immigration) into the green beetle population. This movement of individuals allows for the transfer of alleles between populations, which can introduce new genetic variation into a population and reduce the genetic differences between separate groups over time.

u5.title: Nervous System with their Brief Functions
u5.description: A hierarchical flowchart diagram of the nervous system organization. The Central Nervous System (CNS) in a pink box shows the brain and spinal cord with bidirectional arrows indicating communication. The Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) in a yellow box is subdivided into sensory (afferent) nerves and motor (efferent) nerves. Sensory nerves branch into somatic sensory nerves (carrying signals from skin, joints, muscles) and visceral sensory nerves (carrying signals from body organs). Motor nerves split into somatic motor nerves (voluntary signals to skeletal muscles) and autonomic motor nerves (involuntary signals to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands), which further divide into sympathetic division (fight or flight) and parasympathetic division (rest and digest).

u5.title: Parts of a Neuron
u5.description: A detailed anatomical diagram showing the key structural components of a neuron. The upper portion displays a neuron cell body with a nucleus (purple center) surrounded by branching dendrites that receive signals. A single axon extends downward from the cell body. The middle section illustrates a cross-section of the axon showing the myelin sheath (blue insulation) and Schwann cells that wrap around the axon. The diagram labels key regions: nodes of Ranvier (gaps in myelin between Schwann cells), the myelin sheath itself, and the overall axon structure. The right side includes a cross-sectional view of the myelinated axon showing the myelin sheath surrounding the axon core.

u5.title: Types of Neurons
u5.description: A comprehensive diagram comparing three functional neuron types within their respective nervous system divisions. On the left (pink box) is an interneuron in the central nervous system (spinal cord), showing a central cell body with extensive dendritic branches and a central axon. In the middle (yellow box) is an afferent (sensory) neuron with cell body, dendrites receiving signals from a sensory receptor, a central axon, and peripheral axon fiber connecting to the CNS. The right side shows an efferent (motor) neuron with cell body in the spinal cord, an axon (efferent fiber) extending to an effector organ (muscle or gland), and axon terminals. Color-coded boxes highlight the specialized functions of each neuron type.

u5.title: Resting Potential
u5.description: A detailed illustration of the resting membrane potential in a neuron. The top shows an axon with a recording electrode inside showing -65 mV and a reference electrode outside, demonstrating the voltage difference across the axial membrane. The middle section depicts the axonal membrane with embedded ion channels (shown in orange, pink, and blue). The bottom magnified view shows the distribution of ions: K+ (potassium, pink circles) and Na+ (sodium, orange squares) are concentrated inside the axon, with gated K+ channels (blue) and gated Na+ channels (orange) embedded in the phospholipid bilayer. The diagram illustrates how the sodium-potassium pump and selective membrane permeability maintain the resting potential of approximately -65 mV.

u5.title: Action Potential Begins: Depolarization Occurs
u5.description: A diagram illustrating the initial phase of action potential generation. The top shows a measuring device displaying +40 mV indicating the peak depolarization. An axonal segment is depicted showing the direction of impulse propagation with charge distribution. The lower magnified section shows the axonal membrane with multiple open Na+ channels (depicted as open blue channels among closed ones). Orange and pink ions are shown both inside and outside the membrane. This diagram demonstrates how depolarization occurs when a stimulus causes Na+ channels to open, allowing sodium ions to flow into the axon, reversing the membrane potential and initiating the action potential.

u5.title: Conduction of Action Potentials
u5.description: A comprehensive graph showing the complete time course of an action potential. The yellow curve tracks membrane potential (mV) on the y-axis from -70mV to +30mV as time progresses on the x-axis. The graph is annotated with five key phases: (1) resting potential at -70 mV, (2) threshold of excitation at -55 mV (marked with dashed line), (3) peak action potential at +30 mV, (4) hyperpolarization phase where potential becomes more negative than resting level, and (5) return to resting potential. The diagram effectively illustrates the rapid depolarization phase, the brief peak, and the slower repolarization and hyperpolarization phases that characterize action potential propagation along the axon.

u5.title: Action Potential Ends (A) and Action Potential Graph (B)
u5.description: A two-part comparison showing: (A) The concluding phase of action potential with a measurement display showing the membrane potential, depicting the axon with open K+ channels (shown in blue) allowing potassium ions to flow out, returning the membrane to its resting state. Ion channels are illustrated in the cross-sectional view showing the distribution of ions across the membrane. (B) A detailed graph plotting membrane potential (mV) on the y-axis against time (milliseconds) on the x-axis. The graph shows Na+ moving into the axon during depolarization and K+ moving to the axon during repolarization, with labeled phases including threshold, resting potential, and the characteristic spike and recovery curve of the action potential.

u5.title: Synapse Occurs from Axon Terminal to Dendrites or Cell Body of Another Neuron
u5.description: A comprehensive illustration showing synaptic structure and function. Part (A) depicts a central neuron cell body receiving multiple synaptic inputs from presynaptic neurons. The axons of presynaptic neurons approach and form synapses on the dendrites and cell body of the postsynaptic neuron. An enlarged inset shows the synaptic cleft detail with vesicles and the junction between neurons. Yellow arrows indicate the direction of impulse conduction through axons and across synapses. Part (B) provides a simplified diagram showing the basic pathway: cell body, axon, synapse, synaptic cleft, and direction of impulse conduction, illustrating the one-way transmission of neural signals across the synapse.

u5.title: Signal Transmission Through a Synapse
u5.description: A detailed step-by-step illustration of synaptic transmission showing six numbered stages: (1) Action potential reaches the axon terminal, (2) Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open in response to depolarization, (3) Calcium ions enter the axon terminal through the open channels, (4) Neurotransmitter vesicles release their contents into the synaptic cleft through exocytosis, (5) Neurotransmitter molecules bind to receptors on the postsynaptic cell membrane, (6) Neurotransmitter is removed from the synaptic cleft. The diagram shows the active zone, synaptic vesicles, and the postsynaptic cell with detailed labels of each component involved in chemical synaptic transmission.

u5.title: Parts of Human Brain
u5.description: A detailed sagittal (side) cross-section of the human brain showing major anatomical structures. The cerebrum (telencephalon) is labeled at the top with its brain tissue visible. Key internal structures include the thalamus (surrounding the third ventricle), hypothalamus, corpus callosum, and pineal gland. The brain stem is divided into three regions: midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. The cerebellum is shown at the back. Additional labels identify the skull, meninges (protective membranes), lateral ventricle opening, third ventricle, fourth ventricle, and spinal cord connection. The diagram demonstrates the spatial relationships of all major brain divisions and their protective structures.

u5.title: White and Gray Matter of a Brain
u5.description: An anatomical illustration comparing white and gray matter distribution in the brain and spinal cord. The diagram shows a human figure on the left with a blue line indicating the pathway of neural information to the brain cross-section. The brain cross-section shows the left and right hemispheres with gray matter (cell bodies and dendrites) appearing darker in the outer cerebral cortex and white matter (myelinated axons) appearing lighter in the inner regions. Below, a cross-section of the spinal cord shows the characteristic arrangement: white matter on the outside (myelinated fibers) and gray matter on the inside (cell bodies) in an butterfly or H-shaped configuration. The diagram demonstrates the opposite distribution pattern between brain and spinal cord and explains the functional organization of neural tissue.

u5.title: The Spinal Cord and Spinal Nerves
u5.description: An anatomical diagram showing the spinal cord and its associated nerve branches. The illustration displays a side view with the brain connected to the spinal cord, followed by the vertebral column outline. The spinal cord is labeled with segments and corresponding spinal nerves identified by letter-number designations: Cervical nerves (C1-C8), Thoracic nerves (T1-T12), Lumbar nerves (L1-L5), Sacral nerves (S1-S5), and Coccygeal nerves. The diagram shows nerve pairs emerging from the spinal cord at each vertebral level on both sides. This illustration demonstrates the segmental organization of the peripheral nervous system and the continuity between brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves.

u5.title: The Cross-Section of the CNS Showing the Position of Grey and White Matters
u5.description: A comparative anatomical diagram illustrating the distribution of gray and white matter in the brain and spinal cord. The left side shows a brain cross-section in the transverse (horizontal) plane with labeled hemispheres (left and right) separated by the midline. Gray matter (containing neuron cell bodies and dendrites) appears in darker regions, while white matter (containing myelinated axons) appears in lighter regions on the outer portions. The right side displays a spinal cord cross-section showing the characteristic H-shaped or butterfly-shaped gray matter in the center (containing neuron cell bodies) surrounded by white matter (containing myelinated nerve fibers). The diagram is labeled with 'Dorsal side' and 'Ventral side' orientations, demonstrating how the spatial relationships of gray and white matter differ between the brain and spinal cord.

u5.title: The Somatic Nervous System
u5.description: An anatomical diagram showing the organization and distribution of the somatic nervous system. The illustration depicts a human body with the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord shown in the center) and the peripheral nervous system extending throughout the body. The somatic nervous system components are highlighted in yellow/orange, showing nerve pathways and ganglia distributed along the body's surface and connecting to skeletal muscles. The diagram labels the Central Nervous System (brain and spinal cord), Peripheral Nervous System components including ganglia and individual nerves extending to all body regions including the head, limbs, and trunk. The visual representation demonstrates how the somatic nervous system provides motor control to voluntary skeletal muscles and receives sensory input from the body's surface.

u5.title: The Autonomic Nervous System
u5.description: A comprehensive diagram comparing the parasympathetic (left side, blue) and sympathetic (right side, red) divisions of the autonomic nervous system. The center shows a detailed anatomical illustration of the human body with the brain at the top and spinal cord running down the middle. On the left, parasympathetic pathways are shown with blue labels and connections via cranial nerves (including the vagus nerve) and spinal nerves to target organs (eyes, salivary glands, heart, lungs, stomach, liver, intestines, bladder, genitals). Each connection lists the parasympathetic effect (e.g., 'Constricts pupil,' 'Decreases heart rate'). On the right, sympathetic pathways are shown in red with effects listed as opposite actions (e.g., 'Dilates pupil,' 'Increases heart rate'). The diagram shows the 'Chain of sympathetic ganglia' along the spinal cord. This illustration demonstrates the opposing yet complementary nature of the two autonomic divisions in regulating involuntary body functions.

u5.title: Path Way for a Nerve Impulse in Reflex Action
u5.description: A schematic diagram showing the basic reflex arc pathway. The illustration demonstrates how a nerve impulse travels from stimulus to response without direct brain involvement. The pathway shows: (1) A stimulus (represented by an arrow labeled 'Stimulus') activating a receptor (shown in a blue box), (2) A sensory neuron (afferent neuron) transmitting the signal from the receptor toward the spinal cord, (3) An interneuron (relay neuron) within the spinal cord processing the signal, (4) A motor neuron (efferent neuron) carrying the signal from the spinal cord to an effector organ (muscle or gland shown in a red box), (5) The effector producing a response (shown with an arrow labeled 'Response'). The diagram shows all components connected through the spinal cord, illustrating the rapid reflex response pathway that bypasses the brain for quicker reaction times.

u5.title: The Reflex Action
u5.description: A detailed illustration of a complete reflex action in response to a pain stimulus. The diagram shows a hand touching a hot object on the left, with pain receptors highlighted in the skin. The neural pathway is traced showing: a dendrite of an afferent (sensory) neuron receiving the pain signal, the cell body of the afferent neuron, the axon of the afferent neuron ascending toward the spinal cord, an interneuron within the spinal cord (shown in the cross-section on the right), the cell body of an efferent (motor) neuron, and the axon of the efferent neuron descending to skeletal muscles in the forearm. The response shows muscle contraction (highlighted in pink) causing the hand to withdraw from the hot object. Directional arrows labeled 'Direction of impulse' show the path of neural transmission. The illustration demonstrates the complete sensorimotor reflex loop from stimulus detection through muscle response.

u5.title: Part of the Human Skin
u5.description: A detailed three-dimensional cross-sectional illustration of human skin anatomy showing all major structural and functional components. The diagram is labeled with the three main skin layers: epidermis (top, light pink), dermis (middle, containing various structures), and hypodermis (deeper layer with fat cells in yellow). Within these layers, the illustration identifies numerous structures including: hair shaft, sweat pore, Meissner's corpuscle (tactile receptor), stratum corneum (pigment layer), stratum germinativum, stratum spinosum, stratum basale, dermal papilla, arrector pili muscle, sebaceous gland, hair follicle, papilla of hair, Pacinian corpuscle (pressure receptor), Ruffini corpuscle (stretch receptor), nerve fibers (yellow lines), blood vessels (arteries shown in red, veins in blue), lymph vessel, sweat gland, and fascia. The diagram demonstrates how sensory receptors, blood vessels, and glands are distributed throughout skin layers to enable sensation, thermoregulation, and protection.

u5.title: The Human Tongue
u5.description: An anatomical illustration of the human tongue showing its structure and anatomical landmarks. The diagram displays a profile view on the left showing the tongue's position in the mouth with reference landmarks including the hyoid bone and frenum (the fold of tissue underneath the tongue). The main view on the right shows the dorsal (upper) surface of the tongue with a detailed representation of its surface texture and features. The tongue is labeled to identify the frenum (connecting tissue on the ventral surface) and papillae (small projections on the tongue surface that contain taste receptors). The illustration demonstrates the gross anatomical features of the tongue as an important sensory organ involved in taste perception, speech, and swallowing.

u5.title: The Main Taste Areas of the Tongue that Has Been Taught for Many Years
u5.description: An anatomical diagram of the dorsal (upper) surface of the tongue showing the traditional (and now largely outdated) taste sensation distribution map. The illustration depicts a tongue-shaped outline with labeled regions indicating where different taste sensations were historically believed to be detected: bitter taste at the back of the tongue (labeled with dashed lines at the top), sweet taste in the center and tip regions, sour taste on the sides, and sweet and salt taste combination at the bottom tip. The diagram uses dashed lines to demarcate these taste sensation zones. Note: Modern neurophysiology has demonstrated that all taste receptors for different taste types (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami) are actually distributed across the entire tongue surface, making this classical teaching map a common misconception.

u5.alt_title: Action Potential Repolarization and Voltage-Time Relationship
u5.description: A two-panel figure showing the final phases of action potential. Panel A depicts the repolarization phase with open K+ channels allowing potassium efflux, shown with a membrane potential reading of approximately -65 mV (returning toward resting). A cross-sectional magnification shows the molecular basis with gated potassium channels (blue) and gated sodium channels (orange) embedded in the membrane. Panel B presents a voltage-time graph with y-axis showing membrane potential in millivolts (-60 to +40 mV) and x-axis showing time in milliseconds (0-8 ms). The curve shows two distinct phases labeled: depolarization phase (rising portion where 'Na+ moves into axon'), repolarization phase (falling portion where 'K+ moves to axon'), labeled threshold line, and resting potential baseline. The graph effectively illustrates the biphasic nature of the action potential and the relative contributions of sodium and potassium ion movements.

u5.title: Internal Structure of Nose
u5.description: A sagittal (side view) cross-section diagram showing the internal anatomy of the nasal cavity. The illustration displays the three-dimensional structure of the nose and nasal passages. Sensory cells (smell receptors) are labeled with red lines showing their distribution on the nasal epithelium. A blue arrow indicates the pathway of air current passing through the nasal passages during breathing. The diagram shows the nasal septum dividing the left and right nasal cavities, and demonstrates how inhaled air comes into contact with olfactory sensory cells. Additional unlabeled structures show the turbinates or conchae that increase the surface area for air-receptor contact, optimizing both olfaction (smell) and air conditioning during respiration.

u5.title: External Structures of the Eye
u5.description: A detailed anatomical illustration of the human eye showing all major external and superficial structures. The image displays the anterior (front) view of the eye with carefully labeled components: the lacrimal gland (under eyelid) located above the eye, upper eyelid and lower eyelid forming the palpebral fissure (the eye opening), eyelashes projecting from the lid margins, outer canthus (lateral corner) and inner canthus (medial corner) where the eyelids meet, the caruncle (small reddish structure at the inner corner), the conjunctiva (transparent membrane covering the white of the eye), the sclera (white of the eye), the iris (colored part of the eye), the pupil (black opening in the center), and the limbus (junction between cornea and sclera). The diagram effectively shows the complex anatomy of the eye's protective and accessory structures.

u5.title: Lacrimal Apparatus in the Human Eye
u5.description: A detailed anatomical illustration showing the complete lacrimal (tear) drainage system of the eye. The diagram identifies the lacrimal gland (green structure located above and lateral to the eye), ducts of the lacrimal gland that deliver tears onto the eye surface, the lacrimal canal (pathway along the eyelid margin near the inner corner), the lacrimal sac (collecting reservoir for tears), and the nasolacrimal duct that drains tears into the nasal cavity with an opening in the nose. The illustration demonstrates the complete pathway of tear production, distribution across the eye surface, and drainage into the nasal system. This functional diagram shows how tears are continuously produced and drained, maintaining eye moisture and lubrication.

u5.title: Extraocular Muscles of the Human Eye
u5.description: A detailed anatomical illustration showing the six muscles responsible for eye movement. The diagram displays the eye in cross-section with the orbit (eye socket) shown at the top. Six muscles are color-coded and labeled: the superior rectus (moving eye upward), inferior rectus (moving eye downward), medial rectus (moving eye inward/nasally), lateral rectus (moving eye outward/temporally), superior oblique (rotating eye and moving it downward and inward), and inferior oblique (rotating eye and moving it upward and outward). The sclera (white of the eye) is labeled, showing the attachment points of these muscles. The illustration demonstrates how these muscles work in coordinated pairs to produce all eye movements including vertical, horizontal, and rotational motions.

u5.title: Anatomy of the Human Eye
u5.description: A comprehensive cross-sectional diagram showing the complete internal anatomy of the human eye. The illustration displays all major structures in their correct spatial relationships: the cornea (clear front covering), iris (colored part), pupil (central opening), lens (light-focusing structure), ciliary body (produces aqueous humor and controls lens shape via suspensory ligaments), sclera (white outer covering shown in blue), choroid (vascular layer in red), retina (light-sensitive layer), fovea centralis (area of sharpest vision), optic disc/blind spot (where optic nerve exits), optic nerve (transmits visual information), blood vessels (providing nutrition shown in red), and the vitreous humor (clear gel filling the eye). The diagram demonstrates the optical and structural organization of the eye as a complete sensory organ for vision.

u5.title: Constriction and Relaxation of Pupil
u5.description: A two-panel comparison diagram showing pupil response to different light conditions. The left panel (yellow background) illustrates pupillary constriction in bright light: the image shows a human eye with a small pupil opening, and below it displays a cross-sectional view of the iris showing contracted sphincter pupillae muscles (the circular muscle fibers that constrict the pupil), labeled as parasympathetic innervation. The right panel (blue background) shows pupillary dilation in low light conditions: the eye image displays a large pupil opening, with the corresponding cross-sectional iris view showing relaxed sphincter muscles and contracted dilator pupillae muscles (the radial muscles), labeled as sympathetic innervation. The diagram effectively illustrates the autonomic nervous system's control of pupil size and demonstrates the inverse relationship between light intensity and pupil diameter.

u5.title: The Rods and Cones in the Retina of Human Eye
u5.description: A detailed comparative diagram showing the two types of photoreceptor cells in the retina. The left side shows a rod cell (for black and white vision) depicted in blue, with labeled components: (a) light-sensitive pigments contained in stacked disc membranes, (b) mitochondria to supply energy for phototransduction, (c) nucleus in the cell body, and (d) dendrites that form synapses with the optic nerve. The right side displays a cone cell (for color vision) shown in purple/pink, with the same four labeled components. The diagram notes that rods are responsible for black and white vision and function in low light conditions, while cones enable color vision and function best in bright light. The structural similarities and differences between these photoreceptor types are illustrated, showing how their distinct anatomy relates to their specialized visual functions.

u5.title: Structure of Human Ear
u5.description: A comprehensive anatomical diagram showing all three divisions of the ear and their components. The left side displays the external ear (outer ear) with the pinna (visible ear structure) and ear canal leading inward. The middle section shows the middle ear containing three tiny ear ossicles: the malleus (hammer), incus (anvil), and stapes (stirrup) that transmit vibrations across the middle ear space. The eustachian tube (auditory tube) connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx. The right side illustrates the inner ear containing the semicircular canals (three fluid-filled loops for balance shown in green), the oval window (where vibrations enter the inner ear), the round window, and the cochlea (spiral-shaped structure shown in blue for hearing). The auditory nerve extends from the cochlea to the brain. The diagram effectively demonstrates the mechanical and fluid-based sound transmission pathway from external ear through to the auditory nerve.

u5.title: The Cross Section of a Cochlea
u5.description: A detailed illustration showing the cross-sectional anatomy of the cochlea, the spiral-shaped structure of the inner ear responsible for hearing. The diagram displays the overall spiral shape of the cochlea on the left side. The magnified cross-sectional view on the right shows the internal chambers and structures: the cochlea is divided into three fluid-filled chambers/scalae by membranes - the scala vestibuli (upper chamber), scala tympani (lower chamber), and scala media (middle chamber). The sensory hair cells are shown embedded in the organ of Corti along the basilar membrane between the chambers. These hair cells detect vibrations in the fluid (perilymph and endolymph) caused by sound waves. The auditory nerve is shown carrying sensory signals from the hair cells to the brain. The diagram illustrates how sound vibrations are converted into neural signals through the mechanical interaction of fluids and sensory cells.

u5.title: The Balance Organs of the Ear
u5.description: A detailed anatomical diagram showing the vestibular system components responsible for balance and equilibrium. The left side displays the overall structure of the semicircular canals showing three perpendicular loops (semicircular canal), the ampulla (enlarged region in each canal), the utriculus, and the sacculus. The right side provides magnified cross-sectional views of two key structures: (1) a cross-section through a semicircular canal showing the cupula (gelatinous structure) with hair cells embedded in it, sensory cells that detect head rotation, and otoliths (crystalline structures), and (2) a cross-section of the utriculus showing the sensory hair cells and otoliths that detect linear acceleration and head position. The diagram demonstrates how these structures contain fluid and specialized sensory hair cells that respond to head movements and gravity, sending signals to the brain to maintain balance and spatial orientation.

u5.title: Differences Between Exocrine Gland and Endocrine Gland and Their Secretions
u5.description: A comprehensive comparative diagram showing the functional and anatomical differences between exocrine and endocrine glands. The left upper section shows an exocrine gland (in blue) with a duct system, indicating that it secretes substances outside the gland through ducts (e.g., lumen of gut). The left lower section illustrates an endocrine gland (in green) with blood supply, indicating that it secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream. The right side displays a human body outline with all major endocrine glands labeled and color-coded in yellow: the hypothalamus (in brain), pineal gland, pituitary gland, thyroid gland, parathyroid glands (behind thyroid), thymus gland (in chest), adrenal glands (above kidneys), pancreas, ovaries (female), and testes (male). The diagram also labels other organs that contribute to endocrine function including the stomach, kidney, and small intestine. This illustration comprehensively demonstrates the anatomical locations and distinctions between exocrine glands (with ducts) and endocrine glands (secreting into blood).

u5.title: Hypothalamus and Pituitary Gland
u5.description: A two-part anatomical illustration showing the anatomical relationship and structure of the hypothalamus and pituitary gland. The upper portion shows a sagittal view of the brain with the hypothalamus (highlighted in orange/yellow in the brain), pituitary gland (small structure below the brain), pineal gland, cerebrum, cerebellum, and spinal cord labeled. The lower magnified section provides a detailed view of the hypothalamus (in orange/yellow) and the pituitary gland, showing the posterior pituitary and anterior pituitary as distinct anatomical regions. The diagram demonstrates the close anatomical proximity and functional integration between these two structures, where the hypothalamus produces hormones and regulates the pituitary gland's secretion. This illustration clearly shows how the hypothalamus sits immediately above and controls the pituitary, forming the critical hypothalamic-pituitary axis that regulates hormone secretion throughout the endocrine system.

u5.title: Hormones Secreted by Anterior Pituitary Gland
u5.description: A detailed functional diagram showing the hormonal output of the anterior pituitary gland. The top section displays an anatomical illustration of the hypothalamus (yellow) and pituitary gland (pink/red), with portal blood vessels (red) shown connecting the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary, and the anterior pituitary labeled as containing endocrine cells. The diagram shows how hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones travel through the portal vessels to regulate anterior pituitary secretion. The bottom section is organized as a flowchart showing seven hormones secreted by the anterior pituitary (shown in orange boxes): FSH and LH (affecting testes or ovaries), TSH (affecting thyroid), ACTH (affecting adrenal cortex), Prolactin (affecting mammary glands), MSH (affecting melanocytes), and GH (affecting liver, bones, and other tissues). Under each hormone, target organs are listed in blue boxes. The diagram is further subdivided to indicate which hormones have tropic effects only (FSH/LH, TSH, ACTH), nontropic effects only (Prolactin, MSH), and both tropic and nontropic effects (GH).

u5.title: Hormones Secreted by Hypothalamus and Stored in Posterior Pituitary Gland
u5.description: A detailed functional diagram showing the neuroendocrine pathway involving the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary. The upper anatomical section displays the hypothalamus (in yellow) positioned above the posterior pituitary (in pink/red). Neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus are shown with axons (yellow and orange lines) extending directly into the posterior pituitary, carrying neurohormones produced by the hypothalamus. Red dots represent the neurohormones (ADH and Oxytocin) stored in nerve terminals within the posterior pituitary. The diagram shows this is fundamentally different from anterior pituitary control - the posterior pituitary is directly innervated by hypothalamic neurons. The bottom section shows a flowchart identifying the hormones: a general 'HORMONE' category with its 'TARGET', specifically ADH (antidiuretic hormone affecting kidney tubules) and Oxytocin (affecting mammary glands and uterine muscles). This illustration demonstrates how the posterior pituitary functions as a neuroendocrine organ, directly storing and releasing hypothalamic hormones rather than producing its own.

u5.title: The Thyroid Gland
u5.description: An anatomical illustration showing the location and structure of the thyroid gland in the anterior neck region. The diagram displays a front view of the lower face and neck showing the thyroid gland (in reddish-brown) positioned in the anterior neck below the larynx. The trachea is visible as the tube passing through the center. The larynx is labeled above the thyroid, and the thyroid appears as a butterfly-shaped or H-shaped structure wrapping around the anterior and lateral aspects of the trachea. The illustration demonstrates the anatomical relationship between the thyroid gland and adjacent structures (larynx and trachea) in the neck.

u5.title: Parathyroid Gland
u5.description: An anatomical illustration showing the location and positioning of the parathyroid glands in relation to the thyroid gland. The diagram displays a front view of the lower face and anterior neck with the larger thyroid gland labeled in the center (shown in dark pink/brown) and four smaller parathyroid glands (shown in lighter pink/red) positioned behind the thyroid gland. The parathyroids are arranged in pairs on either side - two superior (upper) parathyroids and two inferior (lower) parathyroids. The diagram is enclosed in a rectangular box highlighting the anatomical region. The illustration demonstrates the spatial relationship between the thyroid and the much smaller parathyroid glands, showing how the parathyroids are embedded in or attached to the posterior surface of the thyroid.

u5.title: The Function of PTH in the Regulation of Blood Calcium Levels in Mammals
u5.description: A comprehensive feedback loop diagram showing parathyroid hormone (PTH) regulation of blood calcium levels. The illustration displays a yellow box at the top labeled 'NORMAL BLOOD Ca²⁺ LEVEL (about 10 mg/100 mL)' indicating the target range. Below this are three major response pathways shown with arrows and anatomical illustrations: (1) When blood Ca²⁺ level falls, the parathyroid glands release PTH (shown in a blue oval at the bottom), which stimulates three mechanisms: in the intestines, active vitamin D increases Ca²⁺ absorption from food into the bloodstream (illustrated with intestine image); in the kidney, PTH stimulates Ca²⁺ reabsorption from filtrate and promotes activation of vitamin D (shown with kidney image); and in bones, PTH stimulates Ca²⁺ release (shown with bone image). These three mechanisms raise blood Ca²⁺ level back to normal, completing the negative feedback loop. The diagram effectively shows how PTH maintains calcium homeostasis through coordinated actions on three target organs.

u5.title: Adrenal Glands
u5.description: An anatomical illustration showing the location and structure of the adrenal glands in relation to the kidneys and surrounding structures. The diagram displays an anterior view of the abdominal region showing two large red kidneys on either side of the vertebral column (shown in blue at center). On top of each kidney sits a much smaller adrenal gland (shown in yellow/gold). A cross-sectional view at the top shows the internal anatomy of an adrenal gland with three labeled zones: the outer cortex, the middle layer, and the inner medulla. The diagram includes labels for: cortex (outer layer), capsule (outermost layer), medulla (inner region), right adrenal gland, left adrenal gland, right kidney, and left kidney. The blood supply vessels (arteries and veins) are shown connecting to the adrenal glands and kidneys.

u5.title: Islets of Langerhans in Pancreas
u5.description: A detailed anatomical illustration of the pancreas showing the islets of Langerhans and pancreatic cell types. The left side shows the overall shape and position of the pancreas (in yellow/golden color). The right side provides a magnified cross-sectional view of pancreatic tissue showing multiple islets of Langerhans (circular structures with different colored cells). The diagram identifies three main cell types within the islets: Delta cells (light green), Beta cells (purple/pink cells in central regions), and Alpha cells (red/orange cells on periphery). The diagram also shows: acini cells (yellow cells forming the outer portions that produce digestive enzymes), ducts (tubular structures for enzyme transport), and the overall organization of the islet. This illustration demonstrates how the endocrine (islet cells) and exocrine (acini cells) components of the pancreas are anatomically integrated.

u5.title: Regulation of Blood Sugar Level
u5.description: A comprehensive feedback loop diagram showing the regulation of blood glucose through the coordinated actions of insulin and glucagon. The illustration displays multiple interconnected pathways centered around the liver (in brown at center). When blood sugar is high (pink box at top right), the pancreas releases insulin (orange arrow), which stimulates glucose uptake from blood into tissue cells (shown with cells labeled 'Tissue cells' in pink) and stimulates glycogen formation in the liver. This lowers blood sugar (green box at bottom). When blood sugar is low (green box), the pancreas releases glucagon (green arrow), which stimulates glycogen breakdown in the liver (releasing glucose back into blood) and promotes glucagon release from the pancreas. The cycle also shows that high blood sugar promotes insulin release in a feedback relationship. The diagram includes the liver (with glycogen and glucose labeled inside), the pancreas, and tissue cells with arrows showing the bidirectional regulation of glucose homeostasis.

u5.title: The Hormones Produced by the Testes and the Ovaries
u5.description: A functional diagram showing the hormonal regulation of reproductive organs by the hypothalamus-pituitary-gonadal axis. At the top, two boxes indicate the dual control: 'Stimulates the male secondary sex characteristics and maturation of sperm' (left) and 'Stimulates the female secondary sex characteristics and maturation of eggs' (right). The central illustration shows the anatomical pathway with the hypothalamus at the top, anterior pituitary below it, and the two gonads at the bottom: testes on the left and ovaries on the right. Curved arrows show the feedback loops and hormonal signaling: the hypothalamus signals the anterior pituitary, which releases FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) and LH (luteinizing hormone). These hormones stimulate the testes to produce testosterone (shown on left pathway) and the ovaries to produce estrogen and progesterone (shown on right pathway). The diagram demonstrates the parallel organization of male and female reproductive hormone regulation and the central role of FSH and LH in controlling gonadal function.

u5.title: Hormones Secreted by Ovaries and Testes
u5.description: A comprehensive table comparing the hormones produced by the female ovaries and male testes. The table is organized into five rows: (1) Source shows illustrations of ovaries and testes; (2) Hormone row lists Progesterone and Estrogen from ovaries and Testosterone from testes; (3) Type row indicates all three are Steroid hormones; (4) Target cells row shows anatomical illustrations of the reproductive system and brain (hypothalamus and pituitary) with descriptions of target tissues; (5) Major responses row describes the physiological actions. For ovarian hormones: Progesterone regulates the menstrual cycle and prepares the body for pregnancy; Estrogen regulates the menstrual cycle and maintains secondary sex characteristics in females. For testicular hormone: Testosterone promotes sperm development and maturation, maintains male secondary sex characteristics, and affects the hypothalamus and pituitary for feedback control. The table effectively summarizes the distinct hormonal profiles and their specific target tissues and responses.

u5.title: Pineal Gland
u5.description: An anatomical illustration showing the location and structure of the pineal gland within the brain. The main image displays a sagittal (side) cross-section of the brain showing major structures with the pineal gland labeled as a small structure in the upper central region of the brain. The diagram identifies surrounding structures including the thalamus (large central structure below and anterior to pineal), and hypothalamus. At the bottom of the illustration is a full brain sagittal view that provides the broader context, showing the pineal gland's position deep within the brain, approximately at the level of the third ventricle. The diagram demonstrates the pineal gland's small size and its central location in relation to other major brain structures, establishing its anatomical position within the diencephalon.

u5.title: Pineal Gland
u5.description: A detailed functional diagram showing the pineal gland's role in circadian rhythm regulation and melatonin production. The illustration displays a brain in sagittal view with the pineal gland highlighted (in pink/red at the center). The diagram shows the neural pathway: light information from the eye (represented by a sun symbol for day and moon symbol for night on the left) travels to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus, which receives light input signals. From there, neural pathways (shown as dashed lines) descend through the superior cervical ganglion (shown at the bottom) to reach the pineal gland. The diagram demonstrates that: (1) During the day (light period), the SCN inhibits melatonin production (shown with red inhibition arrows), and (2) During the night (dark period), the SCN removes inhibition and stimulates melatonin production (shown with green stimulation arrows). A chemical structure of melatonin is shown in a tan box at the top right, displaying the molecular composition. This illustration effectively demonstrates how light-dark cycles regulate melatonin secretion through the neural pathway from retina to SCN to pineal gland.

u5.title: Thymus Gland
u5.description: An anatomical illustration showing the location and structure of the thymus gland within the thoracic cavity. The diagram displays an anterior (front) view of the upper torso and chest showing the thymus gland (in pink) positioned in the anterior mediastinum, between the two lungs. The thyroid gland is labeled at the top of the diagram with the trachea running centrally. The left and right lungs are shown in light blue on either side of the thymus. The heart is visible at the bottom (shown in orange/yellow). The diagram demonstrates the anatomical position of the thymus gland in the mediastinum, its relationship to adjacent structures (lungs, heart, trachea, thyroid), and its size relative to other thoracic structures. The thymus is a lymphoid organ that is prominent in infants and children but involutes (shrinks) with age.

u5.title: The Anatomy of Human Kidneys
u5.description: An anatomical illustration showing the structure and external anatomy of the human kidney. The left side displays the position of the kidneys within the abdominal cavity and their relationship to the spine and major blood vessels. The right side shows a detailed cross-sectional anatomy of a single kidney with all major structures labeled: the renal cortex (outer layer, in light color), renal medulla (middle regions organized into pyramids with a striped appearance), renal pelvis (funnel-shaped structure at the hilum collecting urine), calyces (cup-shaped structures receiving urine from pyramid tips), renal artery (red vessel bringing blood into the kidney), renal vein (blue vessel draining blood from the kidney), and ureter (tube carrying urine from the kidney to the bladder).
